notes: The childhood scenes are in src/simulation/opening-life-content.ts. Each has a premise, a cast (guardian, sibling, peer, housemate) and two to four choices with an aftermath line. Example: a peer offers to swap snacks after the lunch monitor said not to; the child can swap quietly, say trading isn't allowed, or keep their own snack.

Playing a scene with somebody is now recorded as contact between the two of them, and moves nothing. The missing piece is per choice: whether it moves any of the five lines (warmth, trust, respect, commitment, tension) for the other person, and which way.
It is plausible that most choices move nothing and a few matter a great deal. Say so where that is the answer.
Two people can read the same choice differently: the guardian and the peer in the same scene need not agree.

title: What each childhood choice means to the other person in the scene
usableAnswer: A row per scene choice that involves another person: scene key, choice key, and for the other person either 'moves nothing' or the lines it moves with direction and significance (minor, meaningful, major). Rows may be grouped by pattern (for example 'keeping an agreed rule with a peer') where the meaning is shared. The scene and choice keys to cover are in opening-life-content.ts.
whyItMatters: A playtest found that childhood choices never change how anyone feels about the player. Choosing to keep a promise to a sibling or tell on a friend reads the same afterward as doing nothing. Writing those meanings by hand would be invented depth, which the owner has ruled out, so this waits on the answer.
